title: Starting Safely at Any Age
bigQuestion: What does a grown-up need to know and do before the first real roll on a skateboard?

story.title: Saturday on the Grass
story.kicker: A forty-year-old buys a board and spends the first hour not rolling at all.
paragraphs: Dana turned forty in the spring. On a Saturday in September she walked into a skate shop with her phone in her hand and a list on it. The list said: board, helmet, wrist guards, knee pads. The clerk asked what kind of skating she wanted to do. She said she wanted to roll to the park with her nephew without falling on her face.

The clerk set two boards on the counter. One was a narrow street deck with small, hard wheels. The other was a little wider, with bigger, softer wheels. He told her to stand on each one on the shop carpet. The wider board felt calmer under her feet. She bought it, along with a helmet that he fitted with her, adjusting the straps until it did not slide when she shook her head.

At the park she did not go near the concrete. She put the board on the grass beside the path, where the wheels could barely turn. She buckled her helmet, pulled on her wrist guards and knee pads, and stood on the board with her knees bent. Then she practiced the thing she was most afraid of. She stepped off and fell on purpose, rolling onto her side and her shoulder instead of reaching out with straight arms.

By the tenth fall she was laughing. A teenager on the path stopped and said that was exactly how his first coach had made him start. Dana wrote two lines in her phone before she drove home: fell ten times, nothing hurt; next week, roll on the path. It was a small goal. She knew she could meet it.
story.think: Why might Dana have started with falling instead of rolling, and what did that choice protect?

lessons.title: Healing Takes Longer
lessons.mainIdea: Adult bodies usually heal more slowly than children's, so preventing an injury is worth more than toughing one out.
reading: A child who breaks a wrist often heals in a few weeks and is back on the playground. An adult with the same break usually needs longer. As people age, bones rebuild more slowly, and muscles, tendons and ligaments take longer to recover after a strain. An adult also has work, family and bills that an injury can interrupt. That is why a grown-up learner treats *protective gear* as part of the board, not an extra.

Many adult beginners carry an old injury, such as a weak ankle, a sore knee or a back that tightens up. That does not rule out skating. It means you start with the gear on, the speed low and the sessions short. If you have a health condition, a recent surgery or a balance problem, a talk with your doctor or a physical therapist before you start is a smart first step.

The goal is *risk reduction*, which means lowering the chance and the size of harm, not removing it completely. You lower the chance of a fall by choosing smooth ground and slow speeds. You lower the size of a fall by wearing a helmet, wrist guards and pads, and by learning how to fall. Both kinds of choices together let you practice often, and practicing often is how adults get better.

words.d: equipment worn to lower injury in a fall, such as a helmet, wrist guards, knee pads and elbow pads
making harm less likely and less serious, without pretending it can be removed completely
a licensed health professional who helps people recover movement and strength after injury

look.title: Two Ways to Lower Risk
look.text: Picture two columns on a page. The left column is headed Fewer Falls: smooth, dry ground; slow speed; a stable board; short sessions before you get tired. The right column is headed Smaller Falls: a fitted helmet; wrist guards; knee and elbow pads; crouching low and rolling when you go down. Every safety choice fits in one column or the other.
look.prompt: Name one choice from each column that you can make before your first session.

check.q: Why does protection matter more for an adult beginner than for a child?
choices: Adults fall more often than children
Adult bodies usually heal more slowly after an injury
check.why: Bones and soft tissues rebuild more slowly with age, so an adult injury usually costs more time.

check.q: What does risk reduction mean?
choices: Removing every chance of a fall
Making harm less likely and less serious
Skating without gear to build toughness
check.why: Risk reduction lowers both the chance and the size of harm; it does not promise zero risk.

check.q: Which choice lowers the size of a fall rather than the chance of one?
check.why: Gear like wrist guards makes a fall less harmful; the other choices make a fall less likely.

lessons.title: A Helmet That Fits
lessons.mainIdea: A helmet protects you only if it is made for the job, sits level on your forehead and is buckled snug every time.
reading: A helmet works by spreading out and slowing down the hit to your head. Inside the hard shell is a foam *liner* that crushes or compresses when it strikes the ground. That crushing turns a sharp blow into a slightly longer, gentler stop for your skull. In the United States, look for a sticker showing the helmet meets a safety standard. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission sets the standard for bicycle helmets, and ASTM F1492 is a standard written for skateboarding helmets. Some helmets are certified for both.

Fit matters as much as the label. First, set the helmet level, with its front edge about two finger-widths above your eyebrows. Next, adjust the side straps so they meet in a V just below each earlobe. Then buckle the chin strap so only one or two fingers fit between it and your chin. Finally, shake your head and open your mouth wide. A helmet that fits stays put and pulls down a little when you yawn.

A common mistake is wearing the helmet tipped back, which leaves the forehead bare. Another is leaving the chin strap loose or unbuckled, which lets the helmet fly off in a fall. Many helmets are built to protect against one hard crash. After a hard hit, follow the maker's instructions, which usually say to replace it even if you see no crack.

words.d: the foam layer inside a helmet that crushes or compresses to soften a hit
tested and shown to meet a written safety standard
the strap under the jaw that keeps a helmet on during a fall

look.title: The Mirror Check
look.text: Stand in front of a mirror with the helmet on. Step 1: two fingers fit between your eyebrows and the front edge. Step 2: the side straps form a V under each ear. Step 3: one or two fingers fit under the buckled chin strap. Step 4: shake your head side to side; the helmet moves with your head, not on it.
look.prompt: Try the four steps. Which one needed adjusting on your helmet?

check.q: Where should the front edge of a fitted helmet sit?
choices: About two finger-widths above the eyebrows
check.why: Level, about two fingers above the eyebrows, covers the forehead without blocking sight.

check.q: What does the foam liner inside a helmet do?
choices: Crushes or compresses to soften the hit
check.why: The liner slows the head's stop over a slightly longer time, which lowers the force.

check.q: What should you usually do after a helmet takes a hard hit?
choices: Keep using it if there is no crack
Tighten the chin strap and keep going
Follow the maker's instructions, which usually say to replace it
check.why: Many helmet liners are made for one crash and can be weakened without a visible crack.

lessons.title: Wrists, Knees and Elbows
lessons.mainIdea: Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries, and wrist guards help prevent them.
reading: When people fall forward, they reach out with their hands. Doctors even have a name for this: a fall on an outstretched hand. The whole body's weight lands on two small joints, and the wrist bones or the end of the forearm can crack. Studies of skateboarding injuries keep finding the same thing. Wrist injuries are among the most common, and *wrist guards* help prevent them.

A skate wrist guard has a stiff *splint*, a plastic or metal strip, on the palm side. When your hand hits the ground, the splint lets your palm slide and stops the wrist from bending too far back. To put one on, slide your hand in with the splint under your palm, then close the straps snug but not tight enough to tingle. If your fingers go cold or numb, loosen them.

Knee pads and elbow pads have a hard plastic cap over a soft cushion. The cap is made to slide on the ground instead of grabbing, so the force spreads out over a longer distance. On a ramp, skaters drop to their knee pads and slide down on purpose. Buy pads that stay in place when you squat and stand up. A pad that slips down your shin protects nothing.

words.d: gloves or sleeves with a stiff splint on the palm side that protect the wrist in a fall
a stiff strip that keeps a joint from bending too far
pads with a hard sliding cap and a soft cushion that protect the knees

look.title: What Safety Groups Advise
look.text: Skateboarders should wear a properly fitted helmet, and protective gear such as wrist guards, knee pads and elbow pads lowers the chance and severity of injury. Wrist guards are especially useful because wrist injuries are so common.
look.cite: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, skateboarding safety guidance
look.prompt: Why do you think wrist guards get special mention?

check.q: Why are wrist injuries so common in skateboarding?
choices: Riders grip the board with their hands
People reach out with their hands when they fall forward
check.why: A fall on an outstretched hand puts the body's weight onto the wrist.

check.q: Which side of the hand does the stiff splint of a wrist guard go on?
check.why: The palm-side splint lets the hand slide and keeps the wrist from bending too far back.

check.q: Why do knee pads have a hard plastic cap?
choices: So the pad slides on the ground instead of grabbing
To make the knees look bigger
To keep the pad from bending
check.why: Sliding spreads the stop over a longer distance, which lowers the force on the knee.

sections.title: Warm Up and Choose a Board

lessons.title: Ten Minutes Before You Roll
lessons.mainIdea: A short, active warm-up gets the legs, hips and ankles ready for the bending and balancing that skating demands.
reading: Skating asks a lot from body parts many adults rarely use hard. Your ankles tip the board, your knees stay bent, your hips turn and your core muscles hold you upright. Cold muscles and stiff joints react more slowly. A *warm-up* is light, moving exercise that raises your heart rate and muscle temperature before the real activity starts.

Many coaches and sports-medicine sources favor a *dynamic warm-up*, meaning exercises that move through a range of motion instead of long holds. Try this ten-minute plan. First, walk briskly or march in place for two minutes. Next, do ten slow ankle circles each way on each foot. Then do ten leg swings forward and back on each leg, holding a fence. After that, do ten easy squats and ten walking lunges. Finish with ten slow trunk turns, hands on hips.

Keep each move gentle and smooth, not bouncy. If something pinches or hurts sharply, skip that move today. Save long, still stretches for after skating, when muscles are warm and you are cooling down. A warm-up also gives your mind a few minutes to arrive, so you start the session calm and paying attention.

words.d: light, moving exercise that raises heart rate and muscle temperature before activity
a warm-up made of controlled movements through a range of motion rather than long holds
the muscles of the belly, back and hips that keep the trunk steady

look.title: A Ten-Minute Warm-Up Plan
look.cite: Example plan; times are suggestions, not a fixed rule
look.prompt: Which part of the plan takes the most time, and what body parts does it work?

check.q: What is a dynamic warm-up?
choices: Holding each stretch for a long time
Controlled movements through a range of motion
check.why: Dynamic warm-ups move the joints and raise muscle temperature instead of using long holds.

check.q: When does the reading suggest doing long, still stretches?
choices: In the middle of a trick
check.why: Long holds fit best after skating, when the muscles are already warm.

check.q: What should you do if a warm-up move causes sharp pain?
choices: Do it twice as many times
check.why: Sharp pain is a signal to stop that movement, not to force it.

lessons.title: A Board That Feels Calm
lessons.mainIdea: A wider deck and softer, larger wheels give a beginning adult a steadier, smoother ride.
reading: Stand on two boards side by side and you can feel the difference. A deck about 8.25 to 8.75 inches wide, roughly 21 to 22 centimeters, gives larger adult feet more room than a narrow deck around 7.75 inches. More room means your feet can sit across the board with your heels and toes near the edges. That makes it easier to keep your weight centered and to feel the board tip under you. These widths are typical ranges, not rules.

Wheels change the ride even more. Wheel hardness is measured on the *durometer* A scale. Soft cruising wheels are often about 78A to 87A, and hard park and street wheels are often about 99A to 101A. Soft wheels squish slightly as they roll. They grip better and roll over small cracks and pebbles instead of stopping dead. Larger wheels, around 54 to 60 millimeters across or more, also roll over bumps more easily than small ones.

*Trucks*, the metal parts that hold the wheels, can be loosened or tightened with the big center nut called the *kingpin*. Looser trucks turn easily but can feel wobbly. Tighter trucks feel steadier but turn less. For a first board, a shop can set the trucks to a medium feel, and you can adjust a quarter turn at a time as you learn.

words.d: a scale that measures how hard a wheel is; skate wheels are usually rated on the A scale
the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and let the board turn
the large bolt and nut in the center of a truck that sets how loose or tight it turns
the flat board you stand on, most often made of seven plies of maple

look.title: Typical Wheel Hardness
look.cite: Typical durometer A values for skateboard wheels; examples, not a single standard
look.prompt: Which wheel would roll over pebbles on a rough path most easily, and why?

check.q: What does the durometer scale measure on a skateboard wheel?
check.why: Durometer A ratings tell how hard a wheel is, from about 78A (soft) to about 101A (hard).

check.q: Why do softer wheels help a beginner on a rough path?
choices: They squish and roll over small cracks and pebbles
They spin faster on smooth floors
They turn the board by themselves
check.why: A soft wheel deforms a little, so it grips and rolls over small objects.

check.q: What happens when you loosen the kingpin nut on a truck?
choices: The board turns more easily but may feel wobbly
check.why: Looser trucks let the board lean and turn more, at the cost of some steadiness.

lessons.title: Cruiser or Standard Board
lessons.mainIdea: A cruiser is built for smooth rolling and getting around; a standard popsicle board is built for tricks and parks.
reading: Most skate shops sell two main kinds of boards for beginners. A *cruiser* usually has big, soft wheels, a shorter or wider shape and sometimes only a small tail. It is made for rolling on paths and streets, carving gentle turns and getting from place to place. A *popsicle* board, the standard trick board, is shaped like a long ice-pop stick, with a raised nose and tail of nearly the same size.

The raised tail is called a *kicktail*. Larry Stevenson received a patent for a kicktail design in 1971, and kicktails made tricks like the kickturn and the ollie possible. If your goal is to ride a skatepark someday, learn kickturns or try an ollie, a popsicle board with medium-soft wheels is a good middle path. If your goal is to cruise, exercise and ride with family on paths, a cruiser may suit you better.

Before you buy, stand on each board on carpet or grass in your skate shoes. Bend your knees and rock gently from toe side to heel side. Notice which one feels steadier and which one you would rather step onto again. Flat-soled shoes help you feel the board, so wear them for the test. Your answer is more useful than any chart.

words.d: a board with large, soft wheels made for smooth rolling and getting around
the standard trick board shape, with a raised nose and tail of nearly equal size
the raised, angled tail of a board, used to lift the front wheels

look.title: Two Boards on the Carpet
look.text: On the left sits a cruiser: short, with a small tail and four fat, soft wheels. On the right sits a popsicle board: long and narrow, curved up at both ends, with small, hard wheels. You step on each and rock heel to toe. The cruiser feels low and cushioned. The popsicle board feels lively and quick to tip.
look.prompt: Write your main goal for skating, then choose which board fits it and explain why.

check.q: What is a cruiser mainly made for?
check.why: Cruisers have big, soft wheels for rolling on paths and streets.

check.q: Who received a patent for a kicktail design in 1971?
check.why: Larry Stevenson of Makaha was granted a kicktail patent in 1971.

check.q: What is the best test before buying a first board?
choices: Pick the board with the brightest graphic
Stand on each board in skate shoes and feel which is steadier
check.why: Standing and rocking on each board shows which one feels stable to you.

sections.title: Learn to Fall Before You Roll

lessons.title: The Shape of a Small Fall
lessons.mainIdea: Crouching low and rolling spreads a fall out, while locked straight arms send all the force into the wrists.
reading: Every skater falls. The difference between a scrape and a broken wrist is often how you go down. A small fall has three parts. First, get low by bending your knees and dropping your hips, so you have less distance to fall. Next, tuck your chin and keep your arms bent and close. Then turn so a large, padded part of your body takes the ground, such as the side of your thigh, your hip, your back or your shoulder, and *roll* with the motion.

The physics explains why this works. Your *center of mass*, the balance point of your body, sits around your belly button. Falling from a lower height means you hit the ground at a lower speed. A long, rolling stop also spreads the force over more time and more body area. A locked arm does the opposite. It stops you in a fraction of a second, all on one small joint.

If you are falling forward on a ramp with knee pads, you can drop to your knees and slide. That move is called a *knee slide*. On flat ground, run it out when you can: if the board shoots away and you land on your feet, take a few running steps instead of trying to stop at once.

words.d: the point where a body's weight is balanced; for a standing adult, near the belly button
to turn with a fall so a wide, padded part of the body takes the ground and the motion continues
dropping onto knee pads and sliding down a ramp to stop safely
landing on your feet and taking running steps when the board shoots away

look.title: Lower Center of Mass, Slower Landing
look.cite: Worked example with g = 9.8 m/s², v = √(2gh), straight drop with no rolling
look.prompt: For the 1.0 m drop, check the number: 2 × 9.8 × 1.0 = 19.6, and the square root of 19.6 is about 4.43. How much slower is the crouched fall?

check.q: What is the first part of a small fall?
choices: Get low by bending your knees and dropping your hips
Jump as high as you can
check.why: Getting low shortens the drop, so you hit the ground at a lower speed.

check.q: Using v = √(2gh), about how fast does a center of mass dropping 0.5 m land?
check.why: 2 × 9.8 × 0.5 = 9.8, and the square root of 9.8 is about 3.13 m/s.

check.q: Why is landing on a locked straight arm risky?
choices: It stops the body very fast on one small joint
It spreads the force over the back
It is the same as a knee slide
check.why: A locked arm stops you in a fraction of a second, putting the force on the wrist.

lessons.title: Falling Drills on Grass
lessons.mainIdea: Practicing falls on soft grass, in full gear and at no speed, teaches your body the right move before you need it.
reading: Grass is a good first classroom. The wheels barely turn, so the board stays mostly still, and the ground is softer than concrete. Put on your helmet, wrist guards and knee pads first, because the drills are practice for real falls. Pick a flat patch with no rocks, sprinklers or holes, and check it with your feet.

Drill one, the sit-down: from standing, bend your knees deeply, reach your hips back and sit to one side, then roll onto your back with your chin tucked. Drill two, the side roll: crouch, turn your shoulder down and roll over your shoulder and across your back, not over your head. Drill three, the knee drop: kneel onto both knee pads, then let your forearms come down bent, with your wrist guards sliding forward. Do five of each, slowly at first.

Next, add the board. Stand on it on the grass with your knees bent, then step off forward, backward and to each side, landing on your feet. Finally, lean until you lose balance on purpose and use one of the three drills. A common problem is freezing and going stiff. If that happens, make the next try smaller: lower, slower and with a breath out as you go down.

words.d: a short movement practiced many times until it becomes automatic
a fall in which you turn your shoulder down and roll across your back, not your head
leaving the board on purpose by stepping onto the ground with your feet

look.title: The Side Roll in Slow Motion
look.text: You crouch on the grass beside the board. Your chin tucks toward your chest. You turn so your front shoulder dips toward the ground. Your arm stays bent and close to your body. Your shoulder touches, then your upper back, then your hip, and the roll carries you across and onto your side. You end up sitting, a little dizzy, unhurt.
look.prompt: Walk through the side roll slowly three times on grass. Which part felt hardest to keep relaxed?

check.q: Why is grass a good place to practice falling?
choices: The board barely moves and the ground is softer
check.why: On grass the wheels barely turn and the landing is softer than concrete.

check.q: In the side roll, what should you roll over?
choices: Your shoulder and across your back
check.why: The side roll goes over the shoulder and back, never over the head.

check.q: What helps if you freeze and go stiff during a drill?
choices: Make the next try lower and slower, breathing out as you go down
check.why: A smaller version of the drill and a slow breath help the body relax into the fall.

lessons.title: Finding Your Stance
lessons.mainIdea: Regular and goofy are both normal; your front foot goes over the front bolts and your back foot over the back bolts.
reading: Your *stance* is which foot you put in front. *Regular* means the left foot is in front; *goofy* means the right foot is in front. Neither is better. To find yours, stand with your feet together and have a friend give you a gentle, surprise nudge from behind. The foot you step forward with to catch yourself is often your front foot. You can also notice which foot you would put forward to slide across a smooth floor in socks.

Now set the board on the grass. Each truck is held on by four *bolts* that show on top of the deck. Put your front foot over the front bolts, turned slightly toward the nose, and your back foot over the back bolts or just ahead of the tail, turned across the board. Your feet should be about shoulder-width apart. Bend your knees, keep your back straight and look ahead, not down at your feet.

Rock gently from your toes to your heels. Feel the board tip toward the *toe side* and then toward the *heel side*. That tipping is how a board turns once it rolls. If the board feels jumpy, move your feet closer to the bolts and bend your knees more. If one stance feels very wrong after a few minutes, switch and try the other.

words.d: which foot a skater keeps in front
riding with the left foot in front
riding with the right foot in front
the four bolts on top of the deck over each truck; a guide for where to put your feet
the edge of the board under your toes
the edge of the board under your heels

look.title: Feet on the Bolts
look.text: Look down at the board on the grass. Four small bolt heads sit near the nose and four near the tail. Your front foot covers the front four, angled a little toward the nose. Your back foot covers the back four, straight across the board. Your knees are bent like you are about to sit on a high stool. Your eyes look out past the nose.
look.prompt: Stand in both stances on grass for one minute each. Which one lets you rock toe to heel more smoothly?

check.q: What does goofy stance mean?
choices: Riding with the left foot in front
Riding with both feet on the tail
Riding with the right foot in front
check.why: Goofy is right foot forward; regular is left foot forward. Both are normal.

check.q: Where does your back foot go when you first stand on the board?
choices: Over the back bolts or just ahead of the tail
check.why: The front foot goes over the front bolts and the back foot over the back bolts.

check.q: What makes a rolling board turn?
choices: Tipping it toward the toe side or heel side
check.why: Leaning toward the toe or heel edge tips the deck, and the trucks steer the wheels.

lessons.title: Quiet Times at the Park
lessons.mainIdea: Going when a skatepark is less crowded and learning its unwritten rules make the first visits calmer and safer.
reading: Before a skatepark, practice on smooth, dry ground away from cars: an empty tennis court, a basketball court where skating is allowed, or a smooth path in a park. Check posted rules first. When you are ready for a skatepark, timing helps. Many parks are quieter on weekday mornings and early afternoons, when school is in session, and busiest after school and on weekend afternoons. Visit once without a board to see when your local park is calm.

Skateparks run on *etiquette*, the unwritten rules people follow. Skaters take turns at each ramp or obstacle. Watch who is next and wait, then go when the space is clear. Cutting in front of someone's turn is called *snaking*, and people notice. Do not sit or stand in a landing zone, the area where people come down from a trick. Keep your board under control, and if it shoots away, call out so others can step aside.

A beginner belongs at the park. Pick a flat corner or a low, gentle bank and stay out of the main lines, the paths skaters ride through the park. Many skaters are glad to give a tip if you ask between their turns. Wearing pads at a park is normal and common among adults, so leave them on.

words.d: the unwritten rules of polite, safe behavior in a shared place
slang for cutting in front of someone else's turn at a skatepark
the area where skaters come down after a trick or drop
the path a skater rides through a park, linking ramps and obstacles

look.title: Reading the Park
look.text: It is ten o'clock on a Tuesday morning. Three skaters ride the bowl on the far side. One rides a ledge near the middle. The flat area by the gate is empty except for a painted curb. A water fountain stands near a bench. Nobody is waiting at the low bank by the fence.
look.prompt: Where in this park would you practice first, and where would you avoid standing?

check.q: What does snaking mean at a skatepark?
choices: Cutting in front of someone else's turn
check.why: Snaking is slang for taking someone's turn by cutting in.

check.q: When are many skateparks quieter?
choices: Weekday mornings while school is in session
check.why: Parks are often calmer during school hours and busiest after school and on weekends.

check.q: Why should you not stand in a landing zone?
choices: Skaters come down there after tricks
It is too far from the gate
check.why: The landing zone is where skaters land, so standing there risks a collision.

lessons.title: Small Goals, Steady Wins
lessons.mainIdea: Small, specific goals for each session keep an adult learner safe, motivated and able to see progress.
reading: A goal like learn to skate is too big to measure. A *process goal* names a small action you control, such as five slow falls on grass, or stand on the board on the path for one minute with knees bent. You can meet it in one session, and meeting it builds confidence for the next step. Big goals are fine as a direction. Small goals are the steps toward them.

Here is one beginner ladder. Step 1: falling drills on grass. Step 2: stand on the board on smooth pavement, holding a fence or a friend's shoulder. Step 3: roll slowly while someone walks beside you. Step 4: push with your back foot, then put it on the board over the back bolts. Step 5: stop by dragging the sole of your back foot lightly along the ground, called a *foot brake*. Step 6: make gentle turns by leaning to the toe side and heel side.

End each session while you still have energy. Many adult injuries come late in a session, when legs are tired and attention fades. Ten more minutes is rarely worth a sprained ankle. Write down what you did and the next small goal, so you start the next session knowing exactly what to work on.

words.d: a small, specific action you control and can complete in one session
stopping by dragging the sole of the back foot lightly along the ground
a planned order of skills, each a little harder than the last

look.title: A Six-Week Goal Card
look.text: A card taped to the fridge reads: Week 1, falls on grass in full gear. Week 2, stand and balance on the path. Week 3, roll slowly with a friend walking beside. Week 4, push and put the back foot on. Week 5, foot brake from a slow roll. Week 6, gentle toe-side and heel-side turns. Each week has a box to check.
look.prompt: Write your own first three weekly goals. Make each one small enough to finish in a single session.

check.q: Which of these is a process goal?
choices: Five slow falls on grass in full gear
check.why: A process goal is small, specific and something you control in one session.

check.q: Which foot drags on the ground in a foot brake?
check.why: The back foot comes off the board and its sole drags lightly to slow you down.

check.q: Why does the reading advise ending a session while you still have energy?
choices: Many injuries come late, when you are tired and less focused
Wheels wear out after an hour
check.why: Tired legs and fading attention make falls more likely near the end of a session.

choices: Adults usually heal more slowly after injuries

review.q: What is the chin-strap fit for a helmet?

review.q: Which injuries are among the most common in skateboarding?
review.why: Falls on outstretched hands make wrist injuries among the most common, and wrist guards help.

review.q: Which board setup gives a beginning adult the steadiest ride?
choices: A narrow deck with hard, small wheels

review.q: In a small fall, what do you do right after getting low?

review.q: Where should your front foot go when you stand on the board?

review.q: A center of mass drops 1.0 m in a straight fall. Using v = √(2gh), about how fast does it land?
